findings.title: [P1] Restore listener removal in the returned disposer
findings.body: After callers invoke the returned cleanup function, subsequent socket messages still invoke the handler. Long-lived sockets and repeated attach/dispose cycles will retain stale handlers, duplicate processing, and captured state. The previous implementation called `socket.off("message", handler)`, while the replacement is a no-op despite the PR's stated intent to preserve existing contracts.

findings.title: [P1] Restore listener removal in the returned disposer
findings.body:
Calling the returned cleanup function no longer detaches the `"message"` handler. Any message emitted afterward still invokes a supposedly disposed callback, and repeated attach/dispose cycles accumulate listeners, causing stale updates and leaks.

_Recommend validating this comment independently._

findings.title: [P1] Restore listener removal in the returned cleanup function
findings.body:
Any caller invoking the returned disposer expects the registered `"message"` handler to be detached. The no-op leaves it active, so later messages still invoke disposed handlers and repeated attach/dispose cycles accumulate listeners and memory.

_Recommend validating this comment independently._

findings.title: [P2] Restore listener removal when disposing the attachment
findings.body:
The returned disposer no longer revokes the message handler. If a socket remains open after logout, authorization changes, or component teardown, an untrusted peer can send another message and invoke a stale handler holding privileged/session-scoped state. Repeated attach/dispose cycles also retain handlers, enabling message-triggered resource exhaustion.

_Recommend validating this comment independently._

findings.title: [P2] Restore listener removal in the returned disposer
findings.body:
When the socket outlives an attachment and callers invoke the returned cleanup function, the `"message"` listener remains registered. Repeated attach/dispose cycles retain handlers and their captured state, cause duplicate processing, and can produce unbounded memory/listener growth on long-lived sockets.

_Recommend validating this comment independently._
